newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah heads higher, baht falls.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah heads higher, baht falls.

text.p: * Indonesian rupiah heads higher despite ample liquidity and impending election as players unload long dollar positions.
* Thai baht eases as players start buying dollars again but flows still said to be limited.
* Malaysian ringgit eases as interbank swaps and interest rates come off.
* Singapore dollar stuck in tight range, upside capped by bid tone of dollar/majors.
The Indonesian rupiah headed higher on Tuesday on selling of the dollar as the country's financial markets remained stable in the build-up to the May 29 general election.
"There should be nothing scary in the election. Whatever bad or good news there is has already been built in," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
Spot rupiah, due Friday because the central bank will have no clearing on Thursday, was quoted at 2,438.5/39.5 at 0420 GMT from an open at 2,437.5/38.5.
Another Singapore dealer attributed the rupiah's strength to unloading of long dollar positions built earlier on fears of widespread violence during the election campaign.

He said operators were also borrowing the rupiah heavily on the forward market, fearing a possible rupiah squeeze by Bank Indonesia if it decided to copy the Thai central bank's recent move to cut off speculators' access to short-term funds.
However, the central bank said there was no such plan.
A Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said he was still uncertain about the market and preferred to stay square for now.
He said the dollar's downside was well supported because some operators were buying the U.S. unit on dips.
Elsewhere, the Thai baht fell below the central bank's mid-rate of 25.80 to the dollar in both onshore and offshore markets as players went back into the dollar.

There was market talk in Bangkok that some U.S. houses bought the dollar outright in active trade, the first time such activity has been detected since the Bank of Thailand (BOT) moved to squeeze out speculators and created a two-tier market earlier this month.
A Singapore-based dealer said the dollar buying seemed to be mainly by interbank players and the amounts did not appear big.
"It was very patchy. I think it's just the interbank players trying their luck again. They'll probably sell it back down later," he said.
The European bank dealer said there were a lot of baht/rupiah trades going through, apparently to exploit the yield differential.
But she added: "I don't see any reason for yield play. Both the baht and rupiah rates have come off. People are probably just buying the dollar/baht and hedging dollar/rupiah."
Some dealers said turbulence from the floating of the Czech crown could have a slight spillover effect on the baht as well.
The BOT was said to have raised its bond repurchase rate after detecting active buying of the dollar.

"It is not a big hike or anything. I guess the central bank only wanted to send a signal to the market that it is ready to intervene and will not tolerate speculative attacks," a dealer in Bangkok said.

In Malaysia, the ringgit slid as interbank swap and interest rates backed off to the levels seen before the last two weeks' turbulence. Forward rates were again trading at a discount to domestic interest rates.

One-month swaps were being quoted at 35/40 points, which translated into an impact rate of 7.3/4 percent, dealers said. A few days ago one-month had touched a high of 500, implying a yield of 20 percent.

Another European bank dealer in Singapore said the market seemed to have calmed down after the interest rate rises caused by aggressive central bank intervention to prevent the ringgit's fall two weeks ago.
Bank Negara Malaysia is estimated to have sold over $1.0 billion, which sharply reduced domestic market liquidity.
Dealers said some stop-loss dollar buying was triggered around the 2.5100 ringgit level after the U.S. unit broke a technical barrier at 2.5055/60.
"There should be good support at 2.5055/60 now and we should trade higher to 2.5130," a dealer said.
Further south, the Singapore dollar gained fractionally from some ringgit/Sing sales but dealers said the Sing dollar looked stuck in a tight 1.4290-1.4310 band against the U.S. dollar.
-- Madhav Reddy in KL (603-201 4813), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221 384-6364), Anchalee Koetsawang in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
